Heydrich’s rise and rule in Prague
Reinhard Heydrich, once a naval officer, rose rapidly through the SS to become chief of the Reich Security Main Office and a key planner of the “Final Solution,” earning nicknames like “the man with the iron heart” and “the butcher of Prague.” As de facto ruler of occupied Bohemia and Moravia, he crushed opposition with mass arrests, executions, and deportations to concentration camps.
​

Operation Anthropoid
The exiled Czech government in London, working with British Special Operations, trained two paratroopers, Jozef Gabčík and Jan Kubiš, to assassinate Heydrich in Prague. After a misdrop near Prague and help from an underground network, they studied his routines and chose an exposed spot on his daily car route as the ambush site.
​

The ambush and Heydrich’s death
On 27 May 1942, Gabčík stepped in front of Heydrich’s open-top Mercedes to fire a Sten gun that jammed, forcing Kubiš to throw a bomb that wounded Heydrich but did not kill him immediately. Heydrich was taken to hospital and died eight days later from his injuries, making the operation technically a success despite the initial mishap.
​

Nazi revenge: Lidice and Ležáky
In response, the Nazis launched vast reprisals, selecting the village of Lidice and later Ležáky for annihilation: men were shot, many women sent to Ravensbrück, most children murdered or “Germanized,” and both villages physically erased. Only a fraction of the original inhabitants survived the war, and the destruction was openly filmed and used as terror propaganda.
​

Betrayal, last stand, and legacy
A fellow operative, Karel Čurda, betrayed Gabčík, Kubiš, and their helpers for money and amnesty, leading the Gestapo to families who had sheltered them and finally to their hideout in the crypt of the Church of St. Cyril and Methodius. After a prolonged battle against hundreds of SS and Gestapo troops, the surrounded paratroopers chose death over capture, and postwar trials executed key collaborators and Nazi officials; memorials at the ambush site and in the destroyed villages now commemorate the assassins, the resistance, and the civilians murdered in reprisals.
​
